article_title: Kindergarten teachers develop phoneme awareness in low-income, inner-city classrooms
citation: Blachman, B.A., Ball, E.W., Black, R.S. & Tangel, D.M. (1994). Kindergarten teachers develop phoneme awareness in low-income, inner-city classrooms. Read Writ 6, 1–18. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01027275
title: 11-week kindergarten phonological awareness intervention program
description: The article evaluates an 11-week intervention in "instruction in phonological awareness" provided in low-income, inner-city kindergarten classrooms by kindergarten teachers and their teaching assistants. The program was implemented with 84 treatment children alongside 75 comparison children, and produced significant post-test advantages on phoneme segmentation, letter name and letter sound knowledge, two of three reading measures, and invented spelling.
requirements: Delivery by kindergarten teachers and teaching assistants over an 11-week period
constraints: Studied in low-income, inner-city schools in an urban district in upstate New York
target_learners: Kindergarten children in low-income, inner-city classrooms
target_learning_goals: Phoneme awareness, letter knowledge, early reading, and invented spelling
key_sources: Blachman, B.A., Ball, E.W., Black, R.S. & Tangel, D.M. (1994). Kindergarten teachers develop phoneme awareness in low-income, inner-city classrooms. Read Writ 6, 1–18. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01027275

article_title: A Comparison of Commercially Available Digital Microscopes for Their Use in Bench-Model Simulation of Microsurgery.
citation: Awad L, Abdi Z, Langridge BJ, Karoshi A, Butler PEM. (2024). A Comparison of Commercially Available Digital Microscopes for Their Use in Bench-Model Simulation of Microsurgery. Journal of Reconstructive Microsurgery. https://doi.org/10.1055/s-0044-1787980
title: 11-criteria microscope-suitability questionnaire with 5-point grading scale
description: The article developed and distributed a subjective questionnaire of 11 criteria assessing a magnification device's suitability for microsurgical training, graded on a 1–5 scale (1 = poor, 5 = excellent). Six criteria are equipment-specific (ease of use and device setup, convenience, physical dimensions, durability, quality, value) and five are microsurgical application outcomes (depth of surgical field, image quality, magnification, illumination, surgical positioning/mobility). Participants graded each device after performing suturing and anastomosis tasks on a synthetic model.
requirements: Participants must first perform microsurgical tasks (interrupted sutures, end-to-end anastomosis) on a synthetic model before grading each criterion
constraints: Subjective assessment; outcomes were analyzed against a binocular table microscope baseline using the Kruskal–Wallis test
target_learning_goals: evaluating magnification tools for microsurgical training suitability
examples: The questionnaire was completed by 31 participants: two consultants, nine surgical registrars, fourteen junior trainees, and six medical students
key_sources: Awad L, Abdi Z, Langridge BJ, Karoshi A, Butler PEM. (2024). A Comparison of Commercially Available Digital Microscopes for Their Use in Bench-Model Simulation of Microsurgery. Journal of Reconstructive Microsurgery. https://doi.org/10.1055/s-0044-1787980
